section.paragraph: In this section we will learn of another method to solve systems of linear equations called Cramer’s rule. Before we can begin to use the rule, we need to learn some new definitions and notation.
section.heading: Evaluate the Determinant of a 2×22×2 Matrix
section.paragraph: If a matrix has the same number of rows and columns, we call it a square matrix. Each square matrix has a real number associated with it called its determinant. To find the determinant of the square matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {a b} \\ {c d} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ we first write it as $$\left| \begin{array}{l} {a b} \\ {c d} \end{array} \right|.$$ To get the real number value of the determinant we subtract the products of the diagonals, as shown.

note.title: Determinant
note.paragraph: The determinant of any square matrix $$\left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} {a b} \\ {c d} \end{array} \right\rbrack,$$ where a, b, c, and d are real numbers, is
$$\left| \begin{array}{l} {a b} \\ {c d} \end{array} \right| = ad - bc$$

row.cell: Subtract the products of the diagonals.
Subtract the products of the diagonals.

section.heading: Evaluate the Determinant of a 3×33×3 Matrix
section.paragraph: To evaluate the determinant of a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix, we have to be able to evaluate the minor of an entry in the determinant. The minor of an entry is the $$2 \times 2$$ determinant found by eliminating the row and column in the $$3 \times 3$$ determinant that contains the entry.

note.source_type: Minor of an entry in 3 × 3 3 × 3 a Determinant
note.title: Minor of an entry in 3 × 3 3 × 3 a Determinant
note.paragraph: The minor of an entry in a $$3 \times 3$$ determinant is the $$2 \times 2$$ determinant found by eliminating the row and column in the $$3 \times 3$$ determinant that contains the entry.

section.paragraph: To find the minor of entry $$a_{1},$$ we eliminate the row and column which contain it. So we eliminate the first row and first column. Then we write the $$2 \times 2$$ determinant that remains.
To find the minor of entry $$b_{2},$$ we eliminate the row and column that contain it. So we eliminate the 2nd row and 2nd column. Then we write the $$2 \times 2$$ determinant that remains.

problem.paragraph: For the determinant $$\left| \begin{array}{rccrccr} 4 & & & -2 & & & 3 \\ 1 & & & 0 & & & -3 \\ -2 & & & -4 & & & 2 \end{array} \right|,$$ find and then evaluate the minor of ⓐ $$a_{1}$$ ⓑ $$b_{3}$$ ⓒ $$c_{2}.$$

row.cell: Eliminate the row and column that contains $$a_{1}.$$
Eliminate the row and column that contains $$b_{3}.$$
Eliminate the row and column that contains $$c_{2}.$$

section.paragraph: To evaluate a $$3 \times 3$$ determinant we can expand by minors using any row or column. Choosing a row or column other than the first row sometimes makes the work easier.
When we expand by any row or column, we must be careful about the sign of the terms in the expansion. To determine the sign of the terms, we use the following sign pattern chart.
$$\left| \begin{array}{l} {+ - +} \\ {- + -} \\ {+ - +} \end{array} \right|$$

note.title: Sign Pattern
note.paragraph: When expanding by minors using a row or column, the sign of the terms in the expansion follow the following pattern.
$$\left| \begin{array}{l} {+ - +} \\ {- + -} \\ {+ - +} \end{array} \right|$$

section.paragraph: Notice that the sign pattern in the first row matches the signs between the terms in the expansion by the first row.

Since we can expand by any row or column, how do we decide which row or column to use? Usually we try to pick a row or column that will make our calculation easier. If the determinant contains a 0, using the row or column that contains the 0 will make the calculations easier.

problem.paragraph: Evaluate the determinant $$\left| \begin{array}{lccrccr} 4 & & & -1 & & & -3 \\ 3 & & & 0 & & & 2 \\ 5 & & & -4 & & & -3 \end{array} \right|$$ by expanding by minors.

solution.paragraph: To expand by minors, we look for a row or column that will make our calculations easier. Since 0 is in the second row and second column, expanding by either of those is a good choice. Since the second row has fewer negatives than the second column, we will expand by the second row.

section.heading: Use Cramer’s Rule to Solve Systems of Equations
section.paragraph: Cramer’s Rule is a method of solving systems of equations using determinants. It can be derived by solving the general form of the systems of equations by elimination. Here we will demonstrate the rule for both systems of two equations with two variables and for systems of three equations with three variables.
Let’s start with the systems of two equations with two variables.

note.title: Cramer’s Rule for Solving a System of Two Equations

section.paragraph: Notice that to form the determinant D, we use take the coefficients of the variables.
Notice that to form the determinant $$D_{x}$$ and $$D_{y},$$ we substitute the constants for the coefficients of the variable we are finding.

Step 5. Write the solution as an ordered pair.
Step 6. Check that the ordered pair is a solution to both original equations.

section.paragraph: To solve a system of three equations with three variables with Cramer’s Rule, we basically do what we did for a system of two equations. However, we now have to solve for three variables to get the solution. The determinants are also going to be $$3 \times 3$$ which will make our work more interesting!

section.paragraph: Cramer’s rule does not work when the value of the D determinant is 0, as this would mean we would be dividing by 0. But when $$D = 0,$$ the system is either inconsistent or dependent.
When the value of $$D = 0$$ and $$D_{x},D_{y}$$ and $$D_{z}$$ are all zero, the system is consistent and dependent and there are infinitely many solutions.
When the value of $$D = 0$$ and $$D_{x},D_{y}$$ and $$D_{z}$$ are not all zero, the system is inconsistent and there is no solution.

note.source_type: Dependent and Inconsistent Systems of Equations
note.title: Dependent and Inconsistent Systems of Equations
note.paragraph: For any system of equations, where the value of the determinant $$D = 0,$$ $$\begin{array}{lcclccl} \textbf{Value of determinants} & & & \textbf{Type of system} & & & \textbf{Solution} \\ {D = 0 \text{and} D_{x},D_{y} \text{and} D_{z} \text{are all zero} } & & & \text{consistent and dependent} & & & \text{infinitely many solutions} \\ {D = 0 \text{and} D_{x},D_{y} \text{and} D_{z} \text{are not all zero} } & & & \text{inconsistent} & & & \text{no solution} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: In the next example, we will use the values of the determinants to find the solution of the system.

problem.paragraph: Solve the system of equations using Cramer’s rule : $$\left\{ \begin{array}{r} {x + 3y = 4} \\ {-2x - 6y = 3} \end{array} \right..$$

solution.paragraph: $$\begin{array}{cccccl} & & & & & \left\{ \begin{array}{r} {x + 3y = 4} \\ {-2x - 6y = 3} \end{array} \right. \\ \begin{array}{l} { \text{Evaluate the determinant} D, \text{using the} } \\ \text{coefficients of the variables.} \end{array} & & & & & {D = \left| \begin{array}{rccr} 1 & & & 3 \\ -2 & & & -6 \end{array} \right|} \\ & & & & & {D = -6 - \left( {- 6} \right)} \\ & & & & & {D = 0} \end{array}$$
We cannot use Cramer’s Rule to solve this system. But by looking at the value of the determinants $$D_{x}$$ and $$D_{y},$$ we can determine whether the system is dependent or inconsistent.

$$\begin{array}{cccccl} { \text{Evaluate the determinant} D_{x}.} & & & & & { D_{x} = \left| \begin{array}{lccr} 4 & & & 3 \\ 3 & & & -6 \end{array} \right|} \\ & & & & & { D_{x} = -24 - 9} \\ & & & & & { D_{x} = -33} \end{array}$$
Since all the determinants are not zero, the system is inconsistent. There is no solution.
